questions.question: Explain how labelling and streaming can affect students' educational achievement.
questions.correctAnswer: Labelling: teachers label students based on class/gender/ethnicity (Becker: ideal pupil is middle-class). Labels become self-fulfilling prophecies (Rosenthal & Jacobson). Streaming: working-class and ethnic minority students are placed in lower streams (Ball). Lower streams = less qualified teachers, less challenging work, lower expectations. The cycle: label -> lower stream -> low self-esteem ->

questions.question: Describe how pupil subcultures develop in response to streaming, using Hargreaves' and Lacey's research.
questions.correctAnswer: Hargreaves: students in lower streams suffer status frustration (loss of self-esteem from being labelled failures) and form anti-school subcultures to gain status through non-academic means (troublemaking, rejecting school values). Lacey: differentiation (labelling by ability) leads to polarisation (students move to pro- or anti-school extremes). This explains why streaming WIDENS the achievement

questions.question: Evaluate whether school processes are more important than external factors in explaining educational inequality.
questions.correctAnswer: School processes (labelling, streaming, subcultures) are important because they actively create inequality during schooling. External factors (poverty, cultural capital) set the starting point but internal factors determine the trajectory. questions.question: Full-Mark Response Evaluate the view that school processes are more important than home background in explaining working-class underachievement. <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: A grade 9 response will: describe home background factors (material deprivation, cultural capital, Bernstein's codes); describe school processes (labelling, streaming, self-fulfilling prophecy, subcultures); argue school processes are more important (they actively CREATE inequality during school - even working-class children who start well are pulled down by labelling); argue home background matters (sets the starting point, affects teacher perceptions); conclude: both interact - home background creates conditions for labelling, but school processes determine whether the gap narrows or widens. Schools have the power to reduce inequality through anti-labelling policies and mixed-ability teaching, making internal factors more significant as a potential lever for change.
